subject: Pediatrics
subtopic: Iron deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency
concept: Nutritional anemia in children is commonly related to iron deficiency; vitamin B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anemia.

content.definition: Anemia caused by inadequate nutrient supply, absorption or increased requirements.
content.explanation: Iron deficiency progresses from depleted stores to iron-restricted erythropoiesis and microcytic hypochromic anemia. B12 or folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and produces megaloblastic hematopoiesis.
content.mechanism: Iron is required for heme synthesis. B12 and folate are required for normal DNA synthesis.
content.clinical_relevance: Pediatric assessment should consider diet, growth, blood loss, malabsorption, inflammation and inherited disorders.
content.diagnosis: Use age-appropriate hemoglobin interpretation, CBC with MCV/RDW, reticulocyte count and peripheral smear. Ferritin and other iron studies assess iron status; ferritin is influenced by inflammation. Macrocytosis or megaloblastic morphology prompts B12/folate assessment.
content.treatment: Treatment is cause-directed: replace the deficient nutrient, correct the dietary or medical cause, and monitor clinical and hematologic response.
high_yield: Iron deficiency is classically microcytic and hypochromic.
Ferritin reflects iron stores but is also an acute-phase reactant.
B12 deficiency may cause neurologic manifestations.
Failure to respond to appropriate iron therapy requires diagnostic reassessment.

yemen_context.relevance: Pediatric anemia assessment is relevant where nutritional deficiency, infection, inflammation and inherited disorders may coexist.
yemen_context.evidence: No Yemen-specific prevalence estimate is asserted.

review_notes: Original pediatric synthesis based on WHO anemia guidance and pediatric hematology review.
